entry.title: Kafka Under the Hood: How the Distributed Commit Log Actually Works

link.title: Kafka Under the Hood: How the Distributed Commit Log Actually Works

entry.content:
Every AI system eventually hits the same wall: your models are only as good, and only as fresh, as the events that reach them. Feature vectors generated a few seconds after a user click, GPU utilization samples scraped off a training node, inference requests and their latencies, token-by-token usage records from an LLM gateway — all of these arrive as continuous streams of facts, and batching them through cron jobs or message queues that silently drop data stops scaling fast. This is the gap Apache Kafka was built to fill, and it is why Kafka sits upstream of so many ML feature stores, real-time dashboards, and telemetry backends (often right next to a columnar sink like ClickHouse).

Kafka’s core idea is deceptively simple: a distributed, append-only commit log. Producers append records to the end of partitioned logs; consumers read them at their own pace by keeping an offset — a pointer into the log — rather than by deleting messages. Because the log is durable and replayable, the same stream can feed a live dashboard, a training-data dump into object storage, and an online feature extractor simultaneously, each with its own position. Fault tolerance comes from replicating each partition across brokers, with a high-watermark defining what has been safely copied and therefore what consumers are allowed to see.

In this post we read the actual implementation on the trunk branch of apache/kafka — the Scala/Java broker core plus its Java clients. Two architecture diagrams follow: a high-level overview, and a detailed map of the classes that carry every message from a producer’s send() call to a consumer’s poll(). All class and line references link into the real sources on GitHub, so you can follow along in your editor.

Overview: records flow from the producer's accumulator through the Sender to the broker's network layer, get dispatched by KafkaApis to the ReplicaManager, land in the UnifiedLog as indexed segments, while the group coordinator tracks consumers. Click any node to open the source on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • KafkaProducer.send, L1027 serializes the record, runs it through interceptors, and picks a destination partition — either one you set, or computed in partition() at L1681.
  • RecordAccumulator.drain, L1083 collects the batches that are ready to go, capped by the max request size per node.
  • Sender.run, L241 is the producer’s I/O loop; it turns drained batches into ProduceRequest RPCs via sendProduceRequest, L896.
  • SocketServer, L71 accepts connections with an Acceptor (L458) and reads and decodes requests in Processor threads (L779), enqueueing them into a bounded queue.
  • KafkaRequestHandler.run, L108 pulls requests off that queue and dispatches them at L167 to the API layer.
  • KafkaApis.handleProduceRequest, L401 is the protocol facade every client request crosses; fetches enter at handleFetchRequest, L568.
  • ReplicaManager.appendRecordsToLeader, L586 checks the ISR and required acks, then routes the write through a Partition to the log.
  • UnifiedLog.appendAsLeader, L1033 appends to the active segment and rolls it when it grows too large (maybeRoll, L2166).
  • GroupCoordinatorService.joinGroup, L1009 runs consumer-group rebalancing and offset commits on the new KRaft-era coordinator runtime.

Detail: the producer's accumulator–Sender–NetworkClient chain, the consumer's delegate split (classic vs KIP-848 async), the broker's network/handler/replication tiers, the segment-and-index storage engine, and the coordinator's service–shard–metadata split.

The Broker: From Socket to Commit Log

The request path is deliberately boring, which is why it is fast. SocketServer (class at L71) multiplexes NIO sockets: one Acceptor per listener (L458) hands new connections to Processor threads (L779) that decrypt, parse frame headers, and enqueue complete requests. A fixed pool of KafkaRequestHandler worker threads — sized by num.io.threads and resizable at runtime through KafkaRequestHandlerPool, L227 — drains the queue held by RequestChannel, L40, and replies travel back through sendResponse, L91.

KafkaApis (class, L95) is the switchboard: produce requests go to handleProduceRequest (L401), fetches to handleFetchRequest (L568), offset reads to handleOffsetFetchRequest (L1029), and group membership to handleJoinGroupRequest (L1390). Each handler validates the request, calls into the right subsystem, and registers a callback that completes the response asynchronously — the handler thread is never blocked waiting for a disk write or a quorum ack.

The replication brain lives in ReplicaManager (class, L154). appendRecordsToLeader (L586) refuses writes if the partition has no elected leader or the ISR has shrunk below min.insync.replicas; the actual append funnels through appendToLocalLog (L1376) into per-partition state held by Partition (class, L163). Leadership transitions are explicit — makeLeader (L590) and makeFollower (L696) — triggered by metadata records from the KRaft controller. Reads flow through fetchMessages (L1665), which can park a fetch and defer the response until enough new data arrives, a trick that keeps consumer latency low without busy polling.

The Storage Engine: Segments, Indexes, Watermarks

One of the bigger architectural shifts of recent Kafka versions is that the log implementation moved from Scala into a plain-Java storage module. The Scala kafka.log.LogManager you find in core is now just a factory (object, L34) that instantiates the Java org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.LogManager (class, L81). That Java class owns the log-directory map — getOrCreateLog at L1239 maps a TopicPartition to its UnifiedLog — and background jobs for retention, flushing, and recovery that kick off in startup() at L771.

UnifiedLog (class, L105) is the per-partition commit log. Leader-side appends go through appendAsLeader (L1033), which validates record offsets, updates the leader epoch, and assigns contiguous offsets; follower-side replication enters via appendAsFollower (L1093). The write itself is delegated to LocalLog (class, L71), whose append at L586 writes into the active segment, and whose flush at L265 fsyncs up to a given offset — this flush boundary is what the recovery-point checkpoint tracks.

Each segment pairs a data file with two sparse indexes. LogSegment (class, L65) decides when to roll with shouldRoll (L167) — segment bytes reached, time rolled over, or index full — and appends records at L250, indexing the first record’s position per write call. The data file is FileRecords (class, L45, note the new record.internal package) backed by a memory-mapped file; append at L249 is just a write at the end, and truncateTo at L321 is what makes unclean leader elections recoverable. OffsetIndex (lookup, L97) maps relative offsets to file positions with binary search, and TimeIndex (class, L54) does the same for timestamps, enabling time-based retention and “read from yesterday 10:00” seeks. Idempotent and transactional producers are tracked by ProducerStateManager (class, L70), which persists sequence numbers as periodic snapshots (loadSnapshots, L184).

The high-watermark is the bridge between replication and visibility: UnifiedLog.highWatermark (L506) reports the largest offset replicated to all in-sync replicas, and the log only exposes records below it to consumers. Log-end sits at L2142; everything between watermark and log-end is written but not yet safe.

Clients: Producers and Consumers

KafkaProducer (class, L251) is a bookkeeping front end for a background machine. Both send overloads (L1027 and L1147) funnel into doSend (L1180), which serializes the key and value, waits up to max.block.ms for partition metadata, and appends the record into a ProducerBatch via tryAppend, L168. Batching is the producer’s main performance lever: linger.ms lets batches fill, batch.size caps them, and compression applies per batch. The Sender thread then drains and ships them, tracking in-flight batches for retries and sequencing.

KafkaConsumer (class, L552) is now a thin facade over two delegates. subscribe (L725) joins a group; poll (L987) simply forwards to whichever protocol you run. The classic delegate (ClassicKafkaConsumer, L117, poll at L657) uses the long-standing group protocol with heartbeats on a background thread; the newer AsyncKafkaConsumer (class, L178, poll at L936) implements the KIP-848 server-side rebalance protocol, moving most rebalance work out of a global lock. Both paths collect completed fetches into ordered records through FetchCollector (class, L51) and talk to the broker via ConsumerNetworkClient (send, L107), which wraps the shared NetworkClient, L89 — the same I/O core the producer uses, with send at L616 and a completion poll at L705. If you have ever wired Kafka into an Airflow DAG, this split matters: the consumer’s poll loop is where streaming and batch worlds hand off.

Group Coordination: The New Java Runtime

Consumer groups have historically been managed by a Scala coordinator embedded in the broker. On trunk that logic lives in a dedicated group-coordinator module. GroupCoordinatorService (class, L166) is the RPC surface — joinGroup at L1009, syncGroup at L1150, heartbeat at L1193, and commitOffsets at L2352 — all returning futures rather than blocking handler threads.

Internally the service routes each group to a shard keyed by the group’s partition in the coordinator’s log, and GroupCoordinatorShard (class, L158) is a deterministic state machine: membership changes and offset commits are first written as records, then applied to in-memory state, which makes group state reproducible after restarts — the same write-ahead-log philosophy as the log itself. Offset bookkeeping ends in OffsetMetadataManager (class, L80), whose commitOffset at L620 produces the records that back the well-known __consumer_offsets topic.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s quickstart path is KRaft-only — no ZooKeeper. To build from source, run ./gradlew jar, then bootstrap a single-node cluster exactly as the README shows:

KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID="$(./bin/kafka-storage.sh random-uuid)"
./bin/kafka-storage.sh format --standalone -t $KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID -c config/server.properties
./bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties

That is a real KRaft controller and broker in one JVM: the storage tool stamps a cluster ID into the metadata log, and the server starts from config/server.properties. From there the official quickstart at kafka.apache.org/quickstart walks you through creating a topic with bin/kafka-topics.sh and exercising the round trip with the console producer and consumer — a two-minute verification before you write any code.

For an AI workload, the natural next step is making your first event a model-relevant one: emit inference requests as JSON keyed by user ID, append feature updates from your training jobs, or ship GPU telemetry from every node. A Python producer (pip install kafka-python-ng or confluent-kafka) needs only bootstrap servers and a topic name to start appending; the durable log means a consumer that crashes loses nothing, it just resumes from its last committed offset. That replay property is what makes Kafka a good complement to Prometheus — metrics answer “how is the system now,” while the log answers “give me every event since last Tuesday.” And when the stream grows into a lake, the same events can be batch-drained to object storage or queried directly in ClickHouse for offline analysis.

Honest Limits

Kafka is not a database: there are no secondary indexes, no queries, no per-key updates — the OffsetIndex exists to reach a position in a file, nothing more. Retention is a blunt instrument configured in LogConfig (class, L65) — time- or size-based deletion of whole segments — so random access to old records is what compaction and external stores are for. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition; choosing a good partition key for your events is a real design decision, and rekeying after the fact is painful. A broker JVM with modest defaults is fine to start with, but cross-AZ replication traffic, segment fsync tuning, and partition counts that now also drive KRaft metadata size all need attention as throughput grows.

The codebase itself carries its own friction: the ongoing migration from Scala core to Java modules means related logic is split across core, storage, and group-coordinator (the Scala LogManager even aliases the Java one), and two live consumer protocols mean any client-behavior reading must check which delegate is actually running. None of that diminishes the engineering here — it is just the price of a system that has been evolving this fast for this long, and reading the sources on trunk, as we did here, is the most reliable way to know what your cluster is really doing.

entry.title: Meilisearch Source Tour: How the Rust Search Engine Works Under the Hood

link.title: Meilisearch Source Tour: How the Rust Search Engine Works Under the Hood

entry.content:
Meilisearch is one of those projects that feels deceptively small from the outside. You POST some JSON documents to it, you POST a query, and half a second later you get typo-tolerant, ranked results with facet counts. Under the hood, though, it is a carefully layered Rust system: an HTTP layer built on actix-web, an asynchronous task scheduler that persists every write to LMDB before acknowledging it, and a search engine crate called milli that owns inverted indexes, facet databases, and vector stores. This post is a source tour of that system, based on a fresh read of the repository at its default main branch.

The layout itself tells you a lot before you read a single function. Everything lives under crates/: crates/meilisearch is the HTTP server you actually launch, crates/index-scheduler is the durable work queue, and crates/milli is the engine core with no knowledge of HTTP at all. That separation is deliberate — milli could be reused by a different frontend entirely, which is exactly what makes the codebase pleasant to navigate. If you have read our earlier tours of Elasticsearch or the pure-Rust Tantivy library, you will notice Meilisearch sits between the two philosophies: more opinionated and turnkey than Tantivy, far lighter than Elasticsearch.

Two diagrams accompany this post. The overview shows the three crates and the main arrows between HTTP handlers, the scheduler, and the engine. The detail diagram goes one level down into the scheduler’s batch creation and milli’s ranking-rule machinery. Every node in the interactive SVG links to the real file on GitHub, so you can keep this page open in one tab and the source in another.

Meilisearch at a glance: the actix-web REST layer turns every write into a queued task, the index-scheduler applies batches to milli, and search reads milli directly. Click any node to open its source file.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at main.rs setup, which parses the Opt configuration, wires tracing, and starts the actix HTTP server. The application itself is assembled by create_app, L137, and setup_meilisearch, L220 constructs the scheduler and auth controller that every handler shares.
  • Index lifecycle endpoints live in one module: create_index, L231 on POST /indexes, plus get, update and delete handlers in the same file.
  • Document writes are handled by replace_documents, L1367, which delegates to the shared document_addition, L1534 helper. Crucially, this handler returns HTTP 202 Accepted — the write has only been enqueued.
  • The enqueuing point is IndexScheduler::register, L930 in the index-scheduler crate, which persists a Task into an LMDB-backed Queue, L129.
  • On the read path, search_with_post, L866 deserializes a SearchQuery, L87 struct and calls perform_search, L1852 synchronously — search never goes through the task queue.
  • The scheduler resolves which physical database a request touches through IndexMapper, L60, which opens and caches per-index LMDB environments.
  • Each index is a milli::Index, L131: a bundle of LMDB databases for word-to-document postings, exact-attribute postings, synonyms, prefix databases, facet trees, and vectors.
  • Query execution bottoms out in milli’s execute_search, L809, with a parallel execute_vector_search, L744 path for hybrid and semantic queries backed by the vector store.

One subtlety worth calling out before the detail diagram: the search path deliberately bypasses the scheduler entirely. Reads run synchronously against the LMDB environment with bounded concurrency — crates/meilisearch/src/search_queue.rs implements a permit-based queue whose capacity you can tune, and main.rs passes it into the app state. Writes, by contrast, always funnel through the task queue even for tiny updates. This asymmetry is the whole design in one sentence: reads are cheap and direct, writes are durable and serialized. It also explains a common beginner surprise — you POST a hundred documents and immediately search for one of them and get nothing back. The task was accepted, not applied; wait for the scheduler to drain its batch and the document appears.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps the onboarding honest: three steps and you have search. First, get an instance — either the hosted cloud offering or a self-hosted binary. Locally, the fastest route is the official install script, which downloads a single static binary:

curl -L https://install.meilisearch.com | sh
./meilisearch

Docker works just as well if you prefer containers: docker run -it --rm -p 7700:7700 -v $(pwd)/meili_data:/meili_data getmeili/meilisearch:latest. With no master key set, the local instance runs in an unrestricted dev mode; setting MEILI_MASTER_KEY switches on the API-key security layer implemented in crates/meilisearch-auth.

Second, add documents. The example from the README creates an index called movies implicitly and sends three records:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:7700/indexes/movies/documents" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary '[
    { "id": 1, "title": "Carol", "genres": ["Romance", "Drama"] },
    { "id": 2, "title": "Wonder Woman", "genres": ["Action", "Adventure"] },
    { "id": 3, "title": "Life of Pi", "genres": ["Adventure", "Drama"] }
  ]'

The response is a JSON object with a taskUid, and this is the moment the architecture we just mapped becomes visible: your curl hit replace_documents, which enqueued a DocumentAddition task and returned immediately. Indexing happens in the background. Poll GET /tasks/{taskUid} until the status flips to succeeded, then issue the third request, a search:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:7700/indexes/movies/search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary '{ "q": "wondre woman" }'

Meilisearch returns Wonder Woman despite the typo in wondre. That is not a gimmick — typo tolerance is a first-class ranking rule computed against the prefix and exact-posting databases you saw in the Index struct. From Python this same flow takes three lines with the meilisearch client package, which makes the engine a natural companion for FastAPI backends and retrieval-augmented applications — add a dedicated vector store only when you need heavier semantic search alongside keyword search.

How Indexing Actually Happens

The scheduler is the most interesting subsystem for anyone writing concurrent services in Rust. Its run loop lives in a dedicated thread (run, L630) and each iteration executes a tick, L168. A tick reads newly registered tasks, groups compatible ones via create_next_batch, L540, and hands the batch to process_batch, L53. Because tasks are persisted in LMDB before the HTTP response is sent, a crash between “accepted” and “indexed” loses nothing — on restart the scheduler replays the queue. This design is why the API can promise asynchronous durability without a separate message broker.

Inside process_batch, document additions reach milli’s write side. The merged change set flows into the parallel indexer entry point extract, L99, which fans extraction work across rayon threads: field ids, word docids, facet values, and — when the index settings declare embedders — document embeddings. Settings changes travel the same road: the update_all, L577 settings handler enqueues a SettingsUpdate task, and the scheduler re-indexes the affected data. This is also where tokenization enters: milli delegates segmentation and normalization to the charabia crate (declared in crates/milli/Cargo.toml), which gives the engine its multi-language coverage including Chinese, Japanese, Hebrew and Latin-script languages.

Search Execution Inside milli

On the read side, perform_search translates the HTTP query into a SearchContext and calls into milli. extract_tokens, L909 splits the user query into terms and builds a query graph — a small DAG of possible words including typo variants. execute_search, L809 then resolves the candidate universe and asks get_ranking_rules_for_query_graph_search, L510 to assemble the rule chain: words, typo, proximity, attribute, sort, and exactness, mirroring the documented default ranking order. If the request carries a sort parameter, resolve_sort_criteria, L651 inserts the sort rules ahead of the relevance rules.

Worth a brief mention too is the federation layer above all of this: the same crates/meilisearch/src/search/federated/ module powers the multi-search endpoint, where one HTTP request fans out into per-index queries and merges the responses with weighted scores. In network mode it can even forward sub-queries to remote Meilisearch instances, which is the project’s answer to read scaling without full distribution. None of that machinery lives in milli — it is pure HTTP-layer composition on top of perform_search, which keeps the engine crate simple and the composability at the API level where it belongs.

Facets are computed by FacetDistribution, L84, which walks the facet-number and facet-string databases restricted to the result universe. For hybrid queries — where the client sends both q and an embedder reference in the request body — execute_vector_search queries the ANN-enabled vector store and merges semantic and keyword candidates through the score-merging logic in crates/meilisearch/src/search/federated/. The detail diagram traces both of these paths end to end:

The detailed view: task registration and batch creation on the scheduler side, ranking-rule construction and facet distribution on the search side, and the parallel extraction stages on the write side.

Honest Limits

Meilisearch makes deliberate trade-offs, and the README is upfront about several of them. It is a single-binary, single-node engine: there is no built-in distributed cluster, and scaling past one machine means using the experimental network/federated search features or sharding yourself. The dataset fits where LMDB fits — indexes live on your local disk, so very large corpora need multiple instances or a distributed engine like Elasticsearch. Note also that LMDB caps the read transaction count, which is precisely why crates/meilisearch/src/search_queue.rs exists to throttle concurrent searches. Async indexing is a feature, but it means writes are not immediately visible — clients must poll tasks, which adds a bit of bookkeeping compared to synchronous engines like Typesense. Finally, benchmark figures in the README (sub-50-millisecond searches, etc.) are the project’s own claims measured on its own workloads under workloads/; treat them as directional, not as independent results. For pure algorithmic detail on inverted indexing in Rust, Tantivy remains the deeper rabbit hole, and for end-to-end local chat-plus-search stacks you can wire an Open WebUI retrieval layer in front of Meilisearch yourself.

entry.title: MinIO Under the Hood: How a Go Object Store Turns Disks into an S3 Cloud

link.title: MinIO Under the Hood: How a Go Object Store Turns Disks into an S3 Cloud

entry.content:
Modern AI and data workloads live and die by storage. Training corpora, checkpoints, dataset shards, model weights, Parquet lakes, backup archives — all of it eventually lands in object storage because that is the one abstraction every tool agrees on. The S3 API became the lingua franca: Spark reads from it, MLflow stores artifacts in it, and Kubernetes operators mount it for everything from logs to datasets. When you need that API on your own hardware — for cost, for data locality, for compliance — MinIO is the open source answer that has defined the category for a decade.

MinIO is written in Go, ships as a single binary, and speaks the S3 API natively rather than emulating it through a translation layer. Point any S3 SDK or the mc client at a MinIO endpoint and it just works. But the genuinely interesting part is underneath the API surface: MinIO takes a pile of ordinary disks (or a fleet of ordinary servers) and turns them into a single highly available namespace that survives disk failures, host failures, and even the silent bit-level rot that plagues long-lived drives. It does this with Reed-Solomon erasure coding, a custom on-disk metadata format, and a quorum-based distributed lock service — all implemented from scratch in the repo we are walking through today.

This post is a source tour of minio/minio at its default branch (master, commit 7aac2a2c5b7c). We traced the request path from the HTTP edge down to the raw disk driver, verified every symbol and line number, and drew two architecture maps. The overview shows the big layers; the detail map goes one level deeper into erasure mechanics, locking, and cluster messaging.

Overview: from the S3 router at the edge, through the ObjectLayer contract and the pool/set topology, down into the Reed-Solomon engine, the per-disk XL storage layer, and the namespace lock service.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at registerAPIRouter, L255, where every S3 endpoint is mounted on a mux router, guarded by s3APIMiddleware, L210. The objectAPIHandlers struct that carries all handler state is defined right there at L68.
  • The write path funnels into PutObjectHandler, L1793, which authenticates, parses headers, streams the body, and calls the backend; reads come back through GetObjectHandler, L717 and HeadObjectHandler, L1012.
  • Both handlers speak to the backend only through the ObjectLayer interface, L246 — a clean seam that lets the same HTTP layer serve single-node and clustered deployments.
  • At boot, serverMain, L746 validates the endpoint list and calls newObjectLayer, L1199, which returns a running backend wired into the global server state.
  • The backend is a stack: erasureServerPools, L52 federates one or more pools, newErasureSets, L352 carves each pool into sets of disks, and the hash placement function hashOrder, L178 decides which disk in a set owns which shard.
  • Object operations execute inside a set: PutObject, L1249 drives encoding and parallel shard writes, while GetObjectNInfo, L203 reassembles data even when some disks are offline.
  • Finally, every shard lands on xlStorage, L98, the per-disk driver whose WriteAll, L2305 and CreateFile, L2092 methods are where bytes actually meet the filesystem, with object metadata persisted in the xlMetaV2 format at L901.

The detail map below adds the machinery the overview abstracts away: multipart upload state, healing, bitrot checksums, the distributed lock stack, peer-to-peer RPC, and the configuration/crypto subsystems.

Detail view: handlers, the object layer, the erasure engine, XL storage, quorum locking via DRWMutex and dsync, grid-based peer messaging, and the config/KMS layer.

From Install to Your First Object

MinIO’s README is refreshingly blunt about its distribution model these days: the community edition ships as source code only, and the recommended install is a one-liner:

go install github.com/minio/minio@latest

You need Go 1.24 or newer. Once the binary exists, starting a server is exactly what you would hope: minio server PATH, where PATH is any empty folder. On first boot the server comes up with default root credentials minioadmin:minioadmin, and the embedded web console is available at http://127.0.0.1:9000 — from there you can create buckets and upload objects with a browser. That single-folder mode is not a toy: it is the same code path — the same xlStorage driver and erasure machinery, just with one disk — that a fifty-node cluster runs.

To exercise the S3 API properly, grab the MinIO Client (mc) and run:

mc alias set local http://localhost:9000 minioadmin minioadmin
mc admin info local
mc mb local/data
mc cp ~/Downloads/mydata local/data/

That is the full loop: alias the endpoint, inspect the deployment, create a bucket, and copy real files in. Everything mc does here translates to ordinary S3 REST calls hitting the handlers in the diagram above — mc mb ends up at PutBucketHandler, L720, and mc cp ends up at PutObjectHandler. For container users, the README documents building a local image with docker build . and running it as docker run -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001 myminio:minio server /tmp/minio --console-address :9001, exposing both the S3 API and the console port. For anything beyond a laptop, the same binary expands horizontally: list multiple hosts and disks on the command line, and MinIO forms pools and sets across them — no separate “coordinator” process to install. Teams that run Kubernetes can pair it with the official MinIO Operator, and it slots naturally next to other self-hosted infrastructure we have covered, from Kubernetes itself to a Hugging Face Hub mirror for model artifacts.

How Erasure Coding Actually Works

The heart of MinIO is not a database or a journal — it is a Reed-Solomon codec. The Erasure struct, L35 holds a data-shard count, a parity-shard count, and a block size, and NewErasure, L42 sanity-checks the parameters (at most 256 shards) before lazily constructing a klauspost/reedsolomon encoder. On a write, Erasure.Encode, L69 streams the object in blocks, splitting each block into data shards and computing parity shards, then fans the shards out to per-disk writers in parallel. Because the code is systematic, data shards are directly readable and parity shards are pure insurance: with 8 data and 4 parity shards per set, any 8 of the 12 disks can reconstruct the object.

Placement is deterministic rather than replicated. hashOrder, L178 hashes the object name into a shuffle of disk indexes, and newFileInfo, L388 records that distribution in the object’s metadata, so every process in the cluster computes the same answer for “where does shard 3 live”. Reads go through Erasure.Decode, L239, which wraps multiple disk readers in a parallelReader and pulls from whichever disks respond fastest, tolerating absent or corrupt shards as long as the read quorum holds.

Two quieter pieces make this production-grade. First, bitrot protection: bitrot-streaming.go wraps every shard in a streaming hash, so silent corruption on any drive is detected at read time instead of being served to users. Second, healing: HealObject, L1060 notices stale or missing shards, reads the surviving ones, re-encodes through Erasure.Heal, L317, and rewrites the damaged disks in place. Together these give MinIO the durability story that a naive “replicate three times” design struggles to match at the same disk cost.

The Storage Layer Beneath

Below the erasure engine sits the XL storage layer, one xlStorage instance per disk. Its methods are deliberately boring — ReadAll, L1829, WriteAll, L2305, CreateFile, L2092, RenameFile, L2997 — because all the intelligence lives above it. Each object is stored as its shard files plus a metadata blob named xl.meta, formatted by xlMetaV2, L901. That format is version-aware: a single xl.meta can carry multiple object versions, per-part information for multipart uploads, checksum records, and inline data for small objects, which lets tiny objects be served without extra file reads.

Metadata correctness is enforced by quorum, not by a leader. erasure-metadata.go implements functions like findFileInfoInQuorum, L289 that gather FileInfo answers from all disks in a set and accept only what a majority agrees on, with helpers like ObjectToPartOffset, L268 translating byte ranges into shard reads. Disk health is probed through calls like CheckParts, L2399. This metadata-is-data philosophy — the same erasure machinery protects object bytes and metadata alike — keeps the system self-describing after any crash.

Locks, Peers, and Cluster Consistency

Object storage looks embarrassingly parallel until two clients race on the same key. MinIO serializes this with a three-tier lock stack. Locally, namespace-lock.go builds an in-process nsLockMap (via newNSLock, L66) that merges concurrent lockers for the same resource. Cluster-wide, the DRWMutex type at L113 of internal/dsync/drwmutex.go implements distributed read/write locks that require a quorum of N/2+1 grants — Lock, L158 blocks until enough remote lockers say yes, and a refresh loop keeps the grant alive during long operations. The quorum negotiation itself lives in internal/dsync, against the NetLocker interface, L23.

Those lockers are wired to real endpoints by newLockAPI, L101, one stub per peer host, and served on the far side by LockHandler, L52. Note what is not here: no ZooKeeper, no etcd, no external consensus service. All intra-cluster messaging — locks, peer REST calls, notifications between nodes — rides on internal/grid, a connection manager that multiplexes typed RPC streams between nodes. The client side of that mesh is peer-rest-client.go (its grid wiring is visible around L49), and the server side is peer-rest-server.go. It is a textbook example of a Go project betting on simple, self-contained primitives.

Where MinIO Fits in an AI Stack

For ML work, MinIO is usually the quiet dependency underneath everything else. It backs artifact stores — point MLflow at an S3 endpoint and every run’s models and metrics land in MinIO buckets. It holds datasets, index snapshots, and analytic extracts that feed engines like ClickHouse, and it gives long-running training jobs a durable place to checkpoint. The design choices we traced above are exactly why: the S3 API means no bespoke client code, versioning means experiments are reproducible, and erasure coding means a disk loss during a week-long training run is an operations ticket rather than a research incident.

Honest Limits

The most important caveat is the one MinIO states itself: as of the current README, the community edition is distributed as source code only, with no maintained pre-compiled binary releases — legacy binaries exist but “will not receive updates”. If you do not maintain a Go toolchain, the Docker-build path becomes the practical route, and production use of self-compiled binaries is explicitly at your own risk under AGPLv3, which also has licensing implications for some commercial embedded uses. Second, this is real distributed systems software: the quorum locking and pool/set topology demand that you think about server counts, drive counts, and network reliability up front; a two-node “cluster” with one dead node is not degraded, it is read-only, by quorum design. Third, capacity planning matters: objects in a set are striped across that set’s disks, so unbalanced sets or pools of very different ages will show uneven utilization — the pool-routing code picks where new objects land, but it cannot rewrite history. Finally, while MinIO is S3-compatible in the ways almost everyone uses, it is not a bit-for-bit S3 clone; exotic IAM corner cases and some newer AWS-only features may behave differently, so test the SDK paths your application actually exercises. None of these are hidden, but they belong in any evaluation.

entry.title: ParadeDB Source Tour: How pg_search Turns Postgres into a Tantivy-Powered Search Engine

link.title: ParadeDB Source Tour: How pg_search Turns Postgres into a Tantivy-Powered Search Engine

entry.content:
Most teams that need full-text search eventually make an uncomfortable choice: keep everything in Postgres and accept the limits of its built-in text search, or stand up a separate engine like Elasticsearch and figure out how to keep two copies of the data consistent. ParadeDB, the repository behind the paradedb/paradedb GitHub organization, makes a third bet — embed a real search engine inside Postgres itself. The project’s tagline is blunt about it: “Just use Postgres. One Postgres for your application data, full-text search, vector retrieval, and aggregations.”

The implementation lives in the pg_search extension, a Rust crate compiled against pgrx that embeds Tantivy — the same Lucene-inspired library that powers Meilisearch-style engines — directly into the Postgres backend process. On top of that engine sits a custom index access method, a SQL-visible @@@ search operator, a planner hook that reroutes queries into a parallel custom scan, and MVCC-aware segment storage that survives Postgres crashes. Apache DataFusion joins the picture for aggregate workloads.

This post is a guided tour of that source tree as of October 2026, based on the main branch. Rather than describe the project from its documentation, we traced the actual code paths: what happens at CREATE EXTENSION, what runs when you write CREATE INDEX ... USING paradedb, and how a WHERE description @@@ 'running shoes' clause becomes a Tantivy query and then rows in your result set. Two diagrams map the moving parts — a high-level overview first, then a deeper walkthrough of the reader, writer, and storage layers.

Overview of the pg_search extension: the extension entry point registers GUCs and the index access method; SQL-level predicates compile into executable query inputs; the access method's build, insert, and scan callbacks drive the embedded Tantivy engine.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • _PG_init, L127 is the extension’s entry point in pg_search/src/lib.rs. It runs when Postgres loads the shared library and wires up the planner machinery before any SQL is spoken.
  • gucs::init, L374 registers the paradedb.* session settings in gucs.rs — dozens of toggles covering custom scans, segment counts, parallelism thresholds, and cost heuristics.
  • bm25_handler, L111 is the index access method handler. It fills an IndexAmRoutine with function pointers for build, insert, scan, delete, and vacuum — this is the moment USING bm25 (and its newer alias USING paradedb) becomes a first-class Postgres index type.
  • ambuild, L38 implements CREATE INDEX: it reads every heap tuple, converts rows into Tantivy documents, and commits them as segments, with parallel builds supported on Postgres 17+.
  • aminsert, L227 keeps the index fresh on ordinary INSERTs. Each indexed row becomes a Tantivy document keyed by its heap ctid.
  • amgettuple, L293 and its bitmap sibling amgetbitmap, L346 are the two ways Postgres pulls matching rows out of the index during an index or bitmap scan.
  • register_planner_hook, L268 intercepts planning so that a search predicate is executed by a custom scan node instead of a generic index scan — the key to top-N ordering and parallel workers.
  • SerialIndexWriter, L211 is the single-writer wrapper around Tantivy that every mutation funnels through; commit, L522 makes written segments durable and visible.
  • SearchIndexReader, L588 opens an MVCC-consistent view of the committed segments and exposes the search, top-K, and estimation entry points used by both scan paths.

The next diagram zooms into the internals: the SQL surface with its pdb helper types, every access-method callback, the planner and custom-scan layer, the Tantivy reader and writer, and the segment storage they share.

Detailed view of pg_search internals. The access-method group shows the build, insert, scan, delete, and vacuum callbacks that `bm25_handler` wires into Postgres; every query shape funnels through `SearchQueryInput` before hitting the Tantivy reader; the writer commits segments that `MVCCDirectory` later exposes to snapshot-consistent readers.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest way to run ParadeDB is the bundled Docker image. The README’s one-liner is:

curl -fsSL https://paradedb.com/install.sh | sh

That script starts a container with the extension preloaded and drops you into a psql session. If you build from source instead, the repo is a standard pgrx workspace: cargo pgrx init to provision a Postgres install, then cargo pgrx install from the pg_search/ directory. Either way, the first SQL statement is the usual extension dance:

CREATE EXTENSION pg_search CASCADE;

The CASCADE matters — pg_search depends on companion extension objects for its pdb schema of helper types. Next, create a table and index it. Following the docs’ mock_items example:

CREATE TABLE mock_items (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    description TEXT,
    category TEXT,
    rating INTEGER
);

CREATE INDEX search_idx ON mock_items
USING paradedb (id, description, category);

A note on naming: version 0.25.0 renamed the index from “BM25 index” to “ParadeDB index” and added USING paradedb as the canonical access method name. USING bm25 still works as a backwards-compatible alias — both names resolve to the same bm25_handler C function in pg_search/src/postgres/mod.rs. Listing the columns inside the CREATE INDEX statement is how you select which fields become searchable; per-field tokenizers and filters are configured with the pdb.field(...) and pdb.tokenizer(...) option helpers you can see parsed in api/config.rs.

Then query it:

SELECT id, description, rating
FROM mock_items
WHERE description @@@ 'running shoes'
ORDER BY rating DESC
LIMIT 10;

The @@@ operator is the whole query language in one glyph. Its right-hand side can be a bare string, or a typed expression built from the pdb schema — pdb.bool_and, pdb.fuzzy, phrase queries with slop, boosts via pdb.boost, and so on. Scoring is BM25 by default, and you can select the score with paradedb.score(id) or get highlighted snippets back. Beyond plain search, the same index serves filters, facets, term aggregations, vector similarity, and even cross-table joins — which is why the 0.25.0 rename makes sense in context.

Inside the Index Access Method

The cleverest structural decision in the codebase is that ParadeDB is not a separate server talking to Postgres over a socket. It is a bona fide Postgres index access method — the same extension point that btree, hash, and GIN use. That is what bm25_handler registers, and it explains why CREATE INDEX ... USING paradedb looks exactly like any other Postgres DDL.

Each callback has a non-trivial story. ambuild calls into create_index at pg_search/src/postgres/build.rs L303, which reads BM25IndexOptions (L409 in postgres/options.rs) to turn index options into a Tantivy schema, then streams every heap tuple through the writer. Inserts go through aminsert and are batched; Postgres 17+ gets an aminsertcleanup callback (L397 in insert.rs) that finalizes the batch when the insert series ends, which also keeps logical replication correct. Deletions during VACUUM land in ambulkdelete (L96 in delete.rs), and amvacuumcleanup (L24 in vacuum.rs) schedules segment merges afterward.

The storage layer underneath is worth appreciating. Tantivy segments are stored on Postgres relation forks through a custom directory implementation — MVCCDirectory at L372 in index/directory/mvcc.rs gives each snapshot of the database a consistent view of which segments exist, so a long-running query never sees a segment that a concurrent transaction hasn’t committed, and a rollback can’t leave phantom segments behind. Segment merges are serialized by a MergeLock (L43 in postgres/storage/merge.rs) so two vacuum workers can’t merge the same segments twice.

Queries: From @@@ to Tantivy

When the planner sees a @@@ predicate, three layers cooperate. First, the SQL surface: the operator’s support functions in pg_search/src/api/operator.rs parse the right-hand side into a pdb::Query value (the typed DSL at L362 in query/pdb_query.rs) and rewrite the predicate into a SearchQueryInput — the central enum at L76 in pg_search/src/query/mod.rs that represents every executable query shape. Second, estimation: estimate_selectivity_and_cost (L780 in operator.rs) asks the reader for a fast doc-count estimate via estimate_docs (L2697 in index/reader/index.rs) so Postgres can cost the plan sanely. Third, execution: the planner hook replaces the plan with a custom scan that compiles the SearchQueryInput into Tantivy queries and runs them over the MVCC-visible segments.

Custom Scans and Top-K

Why not just answer from amgettuple? Because search workloads care about ordering. A web-style query is almost always “top 10 by relevance” or “top 10 by relevance with filters,” and a generic index scan would fetch every match and then sort. The BaseScan custom scan (L112 in postgres/customscan/basescan/mod.rs) instead runs a TopKScanExecState execution method (L63 in top_k.rs) that keeps a bounded heap of the best documents seen so far, often using “fast fields” (stored numeric columns inside the index) to avoid heap fetches entirely. The planner hook also drives aggregate custom scans built on DataFusion, parallel scans that split segments across workers, and a join custom scan for cross-table search predicates. All of these are individually switchable through the GUCs registered at startup.

Honest Limits

Some grounded observations from the docs and code, without invented benchmarks:

  • Not a standalone server. Tantivy runs inside each Postgres backend. You get ACID transactions and one system to operate, but heavy indexing work consumes the Postgres memory and CPU you give it; there are GUCs for writer memory budgets and background merging, but capacity planning is still your job.
  • Index the fields you query. Like any inverted index, only columns listed in the CREATE INDEX statement are searchable. The deprecated key_field option is accepted for compatibility but ignored — new indexes don’t need a designated key column.
  • Renaming churn is real. This repository moves fast: the 0.25.0 access-method rename, per-version migration files from 0.15.x through 0.26.x, and frequent option changes mean pin versions and read the changelog before upgrading.
  • Version floor matters. Current examples in the docs assume ParadeDB 0.26.0 or newer, and some parallel features require Postgres 17 or 18.
  • License. The community edition is AGPL-3.0, with enterprise features commercially licensed — relevant if you embed it in a service.

For context on where this design sits in the ecosystem, ParadeDB is best read alongside the tools it borrows from and competes with: the embedded Tantivy engine we covered in our Tantivy source tour, the classic standalone architecture of Elasticsearch, and the vector-only Postgres extension pgvector, which ParadeDB complements with hybrid search — BM25 and vector similarity from the same index.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of the paradedb/paradedb repository: BM25 indexes, the @@@ operator, custom scans, and the Rust/Tantivy engine inside Postgres.
